title: Cell Structure, Specialisation & Magnification
description: Plant, animal and bacterial cell structures and their functions, specialised cells, levels of organisation, and magnification calculations including millimetre-micrometre conversions for IGCSE Biology 0610.

notes.heading: Animal and Plant Cells: Structures and Functions
notes.body:
📌 The 0610 Core structures — you must IDENTIFY them in diagrams and micrographs and STATE their functions.
Found in BOTH animal and plant cells:
• **Cell membrane** — a partially permeable barrier that controls which substances enter and leave the cell.
• **Nucleus** — contains the genetic material (DNA) and controls the activities of the cell.
• **Cytoplasm** — the jelly-like substance where most chemical reactions of the cell take place.
• **Mitochondria** — the site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy for the cell.
• **Ribosomes** — the site of protein synthesis. (Ribosomes and mitochondria are explicitly on the 0610 Core list — do not assume they are Extended-only.)
Found in PLANT cells only:
• **Cell wall** — made of cellulose; strengthens and supports the cell.
• **Chloroplasts** — contain chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis.
• **Permanent vacuole** — a large sac of cell sap that keeps the cell firm.

🔑 What the examiner wants
Labelling questions use micrographs and electron-microscope images as well as tidy diagrams — practise spotting the nucleus (large, dark), chloroplasts (small green ovals) and the vacuole (large empty-looking space) in real images.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'cell wall' when the label line points at the outer edge of an ANIMAL cell — animal cells have a cell membrane only. Also: mitochondria release energy; they do not 'create' it.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Shared: membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, ribosomes.
• Plant-only: cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts, permanent vacuole.

notes.heading: The Bacterial Cell
notes.body:
📌 The 0610 Core list for a bacterial cell
• **Cell wall** (not made of cellulose) and **cell membrane**
• **Cytoplasm** and **ribosomes**
• **Circular DNA** — a single loop of genetic material
• **Plasmids** — small extra loops of DNA

🔑 The key contrast
A bacterium has NO NUCLEUS: its circular DNA lies free in the cytoplasm instead of being enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus. This is the single most tested difference. Bacteria also have no mitochondria or chloroplasts — but they DO have ribosomes, a cell wall and a cell membrane.

💡 Worked Example
Exam question: 'State two structures present in both a bacterial cell and a plant cell.' Safe answers: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes. 'Nucleus' would be wrong (bacteria have none); 'chloroplast' would be wrong (bacteria have none).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying bacteria have 'no DNA' because they have no nucleus — the DNA is there, as one circular chromosome plus plasmids; it is simply not inside a nucleus.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Bacterium = wall + membrane + cytoplasm + ribosomes + circular DNA + plasmids.
• No nucleus, no mitochondria, no chloroplasts.

notes.heading: From Cells to Organisms: Levels of Organisation
notes.body:
📌 Definitions (the sequence is asked for in both directions)
• New cells are produced by the **division of existing cells** — cells do not appear from nothing.
• A **tissue** is a group of similar cells working together to perform a shared function (e.g. muscle tissue, palisade mesophyll).
• An **organ** is a structure made of several tissues working together to perform a particular function (e.g. the heart, a leaf).
• An **organ system** is a group of organs working together (e.g. the circulatory system: heart + blood vessels + blood).
• An **organism** is a complete living thing — all its organ systems working together.

🔑 What the examiner wants
Be ready to place a named example at the right level: a red blood cell (cell), palisade mesophyll (tissue), a leaf or the heart (organ), the digestive system (organ system). A leaf is an ORGAN because it contains several tissues — epidermis, palisade mesophyll, xylem — working together.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Calling a whole structure a tissue because it is small, or an organ a system because it is important. The test is always 'how many levels of structure are working together?': one cell type = tissue; several tissues = organ; several organs = system.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
• New cells come only from division of existing cells.

notes.heading: Specialised Cells 1: Ciliated, Root Hair and Palisade Mesophyll
notes.body:
📌 The 0610 list of specialised cells — know the STRUCTURE and how it fits the FUNCTION. First three:
• **Ciliated cell** — lines the airways; its surface carries tiny hairs (cilia) that beat to sweep mucus, with trapped dust and pathogens, away from the lungs.
• **Root hair cell** — a long hair-like projection greatly increases the surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil; no chloroplasts (roots are underground, with no light for photosynthesis).
• **Palisade mesophyll cell** — near the top of the leaf and packed with chloroplasts to absorb as much light as possible for photosynthesis.

🔑 How it works — the adaptation sentence
The mark-earning pattern is always two linked statements: name the structural feature, then state the function it improves. 'Root hair cells have a long projection' alone scores nothing; 'a long projection gives a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions' earns the marks.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Giving a root hair cell chloroplasts 'because it is a plant cell'. Only plant cells exposed to light photosynthesise; underground cells lack chloroplasts.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Cilia sweep mucus; root hair = surface area for absorption; palisade = chloroplasts for light capture.
• Always link structure to function.

notes.heading: Specialised Cells 2: Neurones, Red Blood Cells, Sperm and Egg
notes.body:
📌 The remaining specialised cells on the 0610 list:
• **Neurone (nerve cell)** — a long fibre (axon) carries electrical impulses over large distances; branched endings connect to many other cells.
• **Red blood cell** — no nucleus, leaving maximum room for haemoglobin; its biconcave disc shape gives a large surface area for taking up and releasing oxygen.
• **Sperm cell** — a tail to swim towards the egg, many mitochondria to release the energy for swimming, and enzymes in the head to digest a way into the egg.
• **Egg cell** — a large cell with energy stores in its cytoplasm to support the early embryo; its membrane changes after fertilisation to keep out further sperm.

🔑 What the examiner wants
Two-mark questions pair one feature with one function: 'has a tail — to swim to the egg' is the pattern. Note the exception that proves the rule: red blood cells have no nucleus, so 'all cells have a nucleus' is false.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing the gametes: the SPERM is small and mobile with mitochondria; the EGG is large with food stores and cannot swim. Reversed answers are common.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Neurone: long = carries impulses far. Red blood cell: no nucleus + biconcave = more oxygen carried.
• Sperm: tail + mitochondria + head enzymes. Egg: large with energy stores.

notes.heading: Magnification: The Core Calculation
notes.body:
📌 Definition
$$\text{magnification} = \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}$$
Magnification is a ratio — it has NO units. The two measurements must be in the SAME units before you divide; at Core, work in millimetres.

💡 Worked Example
On a micrograph, a root hair cell measures 45 mm across. The real cell is 0.09 mm.
$$\dfrac{45}{0.09} = \times 500$$
The image is 500 times larger than the real cell.

🔑 Rearranging the triangle
The exam also asks for the missing value:
• actual size = image size ÷ magnification
• image size = actual size × magnification
Draw the formula triangle (image on top, actual and magnification on the bottom) and cover the quantity you need.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Dividing before matching units (mixing mm and µm — see the next note), and giving the answer a unit. Magnification ×500 has no 'mm' after it — the units cancel.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• M = image ÷ actual; same units first; answer is a ratio with no units.
• Cover-up triangle gives all three rearrangements.

illustration.alt: A worked magnification example: a drawn plant cell measured at 45 mm beside the real cell at 0.09 mm, with the calculation magnification equals 45 divided by 0.09 equals 500.
illustration.caption: Measure the image, divide by the real size in the same units — the answer is a ratio, so it carries no units.

notes.heading: Millimetres and Micrometres: Converting Units (Supplement 2.2.3)
notes.body:
📌 The conversion (Supplement 2.2.3 — Core candidates work in millimetres only and can skip this note; Extended candidates must convert, because real cells are measured in micrometres while images are measured in millimetres)
• 1 mm = 1000 µm
• mm → µm: multiply by 1000 (move the decimal point three places right)
• µm → mm: divide by 1000 (three places left)

💡 Worked Example 1 (convert, then calculate)
A cell image measures 30 mm; the real cell is 75 µm. Convert: 75 µm = 75 ÷ 1000 = 0.075 mm. Then $$\text{magnification} = \dfrac{30}{0.075} = \times 400$$

💡 Worked Example 2 (answer in µm)
A drawing of a palisade cell is 84 mm tall at ×600 magnification. Actual size = 84 ÷ 600 = 0.14 mm = 0.14 × 1000 = 140 µm.

🔑 What the examiner wants
Show the conversion as a separate step. Mark schemes award a method mark for matching units even if the final division slips.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Multiplying when you should divide. The check: a micrometre is tiny, so the µm number must be BIGGER than the mm number (0.075 mm = 75 µm, not 0.000075 µm).

📎 Key Points to Remember
• 1 mm = 1000 µm; ×1000 going mm → µm, ÷1000 going µm → mm.
• Convert first, then apply M = image ÷ actual.

flashcards.definition: The partially permeable layer around every cell that controls which substances enter and leave.
flashcards.example: Oxygen and glucose pass in; carbon dioxide passes out — all through the cell membrane.

flashcards.definition: The structure containing the cell's genetic material (DNA); it controls the cell's activities.
flashcards.example: Absent from mature red blood cells and from bacteria, whose DNA lies free in the cytoplasm.

flashcards.definition: The jelly-like contents of the cell where most of the cell's chemical reactions take place.
flashcards.example: Reactions that release energy from glucose begin in the cytoplasm.

flashcards.definition: The site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy for the cell. Cells with high energy needs contain many.
flashcards.example: Sperm cells and muscle cells are packed with mitochondria.

flashcards.definition: A tiny structure that is the site of protein synthesis — present in animal, plant AND bacterial cells.
flashcards.example: Cells that make lots of enzymes contain large numbers of ribosomes.

flashcards.definition: A tough outer layer that strengthens and supports the cell; made of cellulose in plants (not in bacteria).
flashcards.example: The regular box shape of plant cells under the microscope comes from their cellulose walls.

flashcards.definition: The plant-cell structure containing chlorophyll, where photosynthesis takes place.
flashcards.example: Palisade mesophyll cells near the top of a leaf are packed with chloroplasts.

flashcards.definition: The large sap-filled sac in a plant cell that keeps the cell firm.
flashcards.example: When vacuoles lose water the cells go limp and the plant wilts.

flashcards.definition: A small extra loop of DNA found in bacterial cells, separate from the single circular chromosome.
flashcards.example: Genes for antibiotic resistance are often carried on plasmids.

flashcards.definition: A group of similar cells working together to perform a shared function.
flashcards.example: Palisade mesophyll is a tissue made of similar photosynthetic cells in a leaf.

flashcards.definition: A structure made of several tissues working together to perform a particular function.
flashcards.example: A leaf (epidermis, palisade mesophyll, xylem) and the heart are organs.

flashcards.definition: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. A ratio with no units; both measurements must share the same units first (1 mm = 1000 µm).
flashcards.example: A 45 mm image of a 0.09 mm cell is at ×500 magnification.

questions.stem: Which structure controls which substances enter and leave a cell?
choices: Cell membrane
Cell wall
Nucleus
Cytoplasm
questions.explanation: The cell membrane is the partially permeable barrier that selects what crosses. The cell wall is fully permeable support, and the nucleus controls activities, not transport.

questions.stem: In which structure does aerobic respiration release energy for the cell?
choices: Chloroplasts
Mitochondria
Ribosomes
The vacuole
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts photosynthesise and ribosomes make protein — both on the same 0610 Core list, so keep the three functions separate.

questions.stem: Which structures are found in a plant cell but NOT in an animal cell?
choices: Nucleus, cytoplasm and mitochondria
Cell membrane and ribosomes
Cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole
Mitochondria and a cell wall
questions.explanation: Only the cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and the permanent vacuole are plant-only. The membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria and ribosomes are shared by both cell types.

questions.stem: Which list correctly describes the structures in a bacterial cell?
choices: Nucleus, mitochondria, cell membrane and ribosomes
Cell wall, chloroplasts, vacuole and circular DNA
Circular DNA inside a nucleus, plus plasmids and cytoplasm
Cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, circular DNA and plasmids
questions.explanation: Bacteria have a wall, membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, one circular DNA chromosome and plasmids — but no nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts or vacuole. The DNA lies free in the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: What is the function of ribosomes?
choices: They release energy by respiration
They are the site of protein synthesis
They control what enters the cell
They store the genetic material
questions.explanation: Ribosomes build proteins — and note they occur in bacterial cells too, unlike mitochondria. Respiration is the mitochondrion's job; storage of DNA is the nucleus (or the circular chromosome in bacteria).

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the levels of organisation in order of increasing complexity?
choices: organ → tissue → organ system → cell → organism
cell → organ → tissue → organ system → organism
cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
tissue → cell → organ → organism → organ system
questions.explanation: Cells group into tissues, tissues into organs, organs into organ systems, and the systems make the organism. Each level adds a new kind of 'working together'.

questions.stem: Which row correctly matches each example to its level of organisation?
choices: Red blood cell — tissue; heart — organ; palisade mesophyll — cell
Heart — tissue; digestive system — organ; leaf — tissue
Leaf — tissue; palisade mesophyll — organ; blood — cell
Red blood cell — cell; palisade mesophyll — tissue; leaf — organ
questions.explanation: A red blood cell is a single cell; palisade mesophyll is a group of similar cells (a tissue); a leaf contains several tissues — epidermis, mesophyll, xylem — working together, making it an organ.

questions.stem: Ciliated cells line the airways. What is their function?
choices: Their cilia beat to sweep mucus and trapped particles away from the lungs
They absorb oxygen into the blood
They produce mucus to trap pathogens
They carry electrical impulses to the lungs
questions.explanation: The beating cilia move the mucus layer — with the dust and pathogens stuck in it — up and away from the lungs. The mucus itself is made by other (goblet) cells; neurones carry impulses.

questions.stem: How does the structure of a red blood cell adapt it for carrying oxygen?
choices: It has a large nucleus to control oxygen uptake
It has a tail to swim through the blood
It has no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin, and a biconcave shape with a large surface area
It has a cellulose wall to protect the haemoglobin
questions.explanation: Losing the nucleus maximises the space for haemoglobin, and the biconcave disc gives a large surface area for oxygen to diffuse across. Animal cells never have cell walls, and no blood cell swims.

questions.stem: Which feature of a root hair cell helps it absorb water and mineral ions from the soil?
choices: A large permanent vacuole that stores soil water
Many chloroplasts to photosynthesise underground
A thick cellulose wall to keep soil particles out
A long hair-like projection that greatly increases the surface area for absorption
questions.explanation: The long projection is the adaptation — it puts a huge absorbing surface in contact with soil water. Root hair cells have no chloroplasts (no light underground), and the vacuole stores sap, not soil water.

questions.stem: On a micrograph, a cell measures 45 mm across. The real cell is 0.09 mm across. What is the magnification?
questions.explanation: Magnification = image ÷ actual $= \dfrac{45}{0.09} = 500$. The units already match (both mm), and the answer is a ratio with no units. ×50 comes from a decimal slip; ×4050 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A drawing of an insect's eye measures 60 mm and the magnification is ×400. What is the actual size of the eye?
choices: 24 mm
6.7 mm
questions.explanation: Rearrange: actual size = image ÷ magnification $= \dfrac{60}{400} = 0.15\text{ mm}$. $24\text{ mm}$ multiplies instead; $6.7\text{ mm}$ divides the numbers the wrong way round.

questions.stem: A cell image measures 30 mm across. The real cell measures 75 µm. What is the magnification?
questions.explanation: Match the units first: 75 µm $= \dfrac{75}{1000} = 0.075\text{ mm}$. Then magnification $= \dfrac{30}{0.075} = \times 400$. ×0.4 divides without converting, and ×2.5 turns the division upside down.

questions.stem: How many micrometres (µm) are there in one millimetre (mm)?
questions.explanation: 1 mm = 1000 µm. To convert mm to µm multiply by 1000 (0.075 mm = 75 µm); to convert µm to mm divide by 1000.

questions.stem: A student's drawing of a palisade cell is 84 mm tall and was drawn at a magnification of ×600. What is the actual height of the cell in micrometres?
choices: 140 µm
14 µm
questions.explanation: Two steps: actual size $= \dfrac{84}{600} = 0.14\text{ mm}$, then convert: $0.14 \times 1000 = 140$ µm. 0.14 µm forgets the conversion, and 1400 µm comes from a decimal slip in the division (84 ÷ 600 = 1.4 mm) before converting.
